prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wages and the regional distribution of employment

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, as one achievement. It explains why labour demand and wages diverge across skill groups and places. It pairs an explanatory framework (skill demand and supply, the race between education and technology, tasks) with transparent quasi-experimental evidence on import competition and local labour markets. That pairing of new evidence and a framework that explains it is what I weigh most heavily, and I would apply it to a candidate from any field. On the chair's questions, as I understand the literature and without independent verification: (1) Katz's distinct, citable contribution is the long-run account of how the supply of and demand for skills moved the wage structure. It runs from the Katz-Murphy work on relative supply and demand, through the work with Autor and Krueger on skill upgrading, to the Goldin-Katz study of education and technology. It is separate from the China-shock identification and from the task model, which is why the citation can be worded around labour demand and wages instead of claiming priority for the task model. (2) The China-shock findings I would anchor on are the persistent local employment losses, their regional concentration, and the limited reallocation of workers and places. The contested parts are the aggregate magnitude, the long-run persistence in some settings, and external validity beyond the US episode. The citation should say 'regional distribution of employment' and avoid any effect size. (3) The 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes reduce the marginal case somewhat. Goldin's prize was on women's labour-market outcomes, Card's on natural experiments, and Acemoglu's on institutions and growth. None of them credited the measurement of how technology and trade shift demand across skill groups and places. The overlap is real for Katz because of his work with Goldin, and I count it as a cost. Round 1 showed broad agreement on the scientific standing of B027, and I do not treat that agreement as merit. What changed for me in this round is the fallback ordering and my alternatives, not the preferred set.
statement.case_against: Attribution under the three-name cap is still the weakest point. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is excluded. Katz's strand is partly separate, so the citation joins two literatures that some members will read as two prizes. The task framework has contributors outside the credited names (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane). The China-shock magnitudes and persistence are debated. Katz's long collaboration with Goldin may lower the marginal case for his share. A two-name Autor-Hanson award would be cleaner on attribution, but it would credit neither the skill-demand strand nor Dorn, and I think it understates the achievement the shortlist item describes. The B027 evidence is also mostly about local and distributional effects. Aggregate welfare claims need more structure than the designs supply.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file moved to Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that a trade-shock-only trio would credit half the achievement and that the citation should be worded around labour demand, wages and local labour markets so the Acemoglu overlap is limited.
responses.response: My round-1 reply addressed your opening trio (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), which your file no longer proposes. On your current position we agree on the set and on the wording strategy. I accept your point that the match between the credited work and the citation, not the number of supporters, is what justifies Katz. I also accept the risk you name, which is that a joint citation may read as two prizes. I would answer it by keeping the citation on demand shifts and regional adjustment, with Autor as the common thread. If the committee decides the citation must be narrower, I would move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a trade-adjustment citation, and I would prefer that to a two-name award.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file moved from B012 to B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He ties the skills-and-technology lineage to capital-skill complementarity and notes that the credit for B012 is crowded by precursors outside the named set.
responses.response: I agree that the three-name set now has broad support in the files, but I do not take that as evidence of merit. I also correct my round-1 reply, which answered your opening two-name proposal. Your file's argument for Katz, that he anchors the skill-demand and supply evidence, is the one I would rest on. Your disclosure of research adjacency in capital-skill complementarity matters here, and I would not lean on your framing of the technology strand more than the evidence supports. Your point on B012 changes my fallback ordering. I still regard Helpman and Melitz as a mature two-person claim, but I put the precursor-credit problem (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) and the adjacency to the 2008 prize against it in a way I did not in round 1.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B006 for Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He cites clean attribution, near-thirty-year maturity and a dynamic propagation mechanism that differs from the 2022 prize. He accepts that the contribution is mainly theoretical with thinner direct identification.
responses.response: In answer to the chair's question, I do not think the weaker direct identification of B006 is disqualifying. It is a reason to rank it below B027 for me, because B027's main claims have been tested against micro data in many settings. Your attribution argument is better than B027's. A Kiyotaki-Moore award has no Dorn-type exclusion and no overlapping task-model authorship. Your distinction from the 2022 prize, that this is a dynamic asset-price propagation mechanism and not a bank-run or intermediation result, is credible and I would accept it in a citation. For that reason I have moved B006 into my alternatives in place of B032. If the committee cannot agree a coherent B027 citation, I would rank B006 and B012 close together as the next options. I do not read your preference as field affinity alone.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Autor, Katz and Hanson for B027, concedes that Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's, and says he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the citation were narrowed to trade exposure.
responses.response: Your conditional support for the Dorn version is the clearest statement of what the Katz-versus-Dorn choice turns on. We agree that the question is the scope of the citation and not the merit of the work. I would make the same conditional move. For the private vote I propose one configuration, Autor, Hanson and Katz, with a joint citation. If the committee prefers the narrower version, I would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation limited to import competition and regional adjustment. I would not do so if the wording still claimed the task model. I am less convinced than you that Dorn's claim is equal to Hanson's. The trade-shock papers are a joint product, and I would not rank the two on the evidence in front of us.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats technology and trade as one achievement (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or only the import-competition work as the discovery (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), and how that choice changes the citation.
How much Katz's collaboration with Goldin (2023) and the Acemoglu overlap (2024) reduce the marginal case for the skills-and-tasks strand.
Whether the China-shock magnitudes, persistence and external validity are robust enough to anchor half of the citation, or whether continuing reanalysis weakens it.

Whether my ordering of fallbacks (a narrow trade citation, then B012, then B006) matches the committee's view of attribution clarity versus empirical confirmation. I have weighed B006 less than members who ranked it in their openings, and I have not independently verified the literature claims I make here.
Whether B032 and B028, which I ranked second and third in my opening, would hold up better under the exchange. Neither was tested in round 1, so I have not changed my view of them on evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No personal, co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I presented Goldin's 2023 prize at the announcement. Katz is a long-time co-author of Goldin, so I disclose this as context for how I weigh the overlap with the 2023 prize, not as a tie to Katz. I am on the Board of Editors of the American Economic Review (2025-), and credited names publish in that journal. I note this as a general editorial role, not a tie to any candidate. My field of labour economics is adjacent to B027 and B028, which I disclose as adjacency only. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
